findings.title: Device is added to the local cache before the store write, so a device rejected at the limit is admitted on its next request
findings.description: `tagDeviceUI` checks the local cache (impl.go:83-85), then calls `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` at line 87 before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` at line 93. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, `tagDeviceUI` returns it, `TagDevice` now propagates it (impl.go:144-148), and `Authenticate` returns it (client.go:44-47). The key stays cached for the 29-minute default expiration set at impl.go:42. The device's next request hits the cache at impl.go:83-85, returns nil, and `Authenticate` returns an identity. A rejected device is therefore denied only once per 29-minute window; a page refresh gets it in. The cache entry should be set only after a successful write, or removed when the write fails.

findings.title: `updateDevice` re-prepends the query to a captured `args` slice on every callback run, so a SQLite lock retry executes with a corrupted argument list
findings.description: `args` is declared at line 80 and captured by the closure passed to `WithDbSession`. Line 84 reassigns it: `args = append([]interface{}{query}, args...)`. Each invocation prepends the query again. `withDbSession` runs the callback through `retryer.Retry` and `retryOnLocks` (pkg/services/sqlstore/session.go:126-127, 86-110), which re-invokes the same closure when SQLite returns `ErrLocked` or `ErrBusy`. On the second run the statement receives seven bound values for six placeholders, so `database/sql` returns an argument-count error. `updateDevice` then returns that error instead of `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. `Authenticate` only logs it (client.go:49) and admits the request, and the device update is lost. The same pattern exists in `CreateOrUpdateDevice` at database.go:150, which this diff does not touch. The fix is to build the exec slice in a new local variable inside the closure.

findings.title: The device-limit check is skipped for any request that omits `X-Grafana-Device-Id`
findings.description: `TagDevice` returns nil at lines 120-122 when the header is empty, before the limit check in `CreateOrUpdateDevice` (database.go:109-118) runs. `Authenticate` then returns an identity (client.go:52-58), so a request without the header gets anonymous access regardless of `device_limit`. The frontend can omit it: `backend_srv.ts:159-162` sets the header only when `this.deviceID` is truthy, and that value comes from FingerprintJS (`backend_srv.ts:97-99`). It stays null if the load throws (`backend_srv.ts:100-101`). Any non-browser client can also leave the header out. Requests without a device ID should be rejected or counted when the limit is set.

findings.title: The count and the insert in `CreateOrUpdateDevice` are not atomic, so concurrent new devices can exceed `device_limit`
findings.description: The limit check counts devices (line 110), compares against the limit (line 115), and only then runs the upsert (lines 120-156), with no transaction or lock in between. Several requests from distinct new devices that arrive together can each read a count below the limit and each insert, pushing the count past `device_limit`. The overshoot is bounded by request concurrency, and it is not bounded at all across multiple Grafana instances sharing one database. The count and insert need to happen atomically.

findings.title: Device tagging now runs synchronously on the request context, so a stalled database write blocks anonymous authentication
findings.description: Before this change, `Authenticate` ran `TagDevice` in a goroutine using `context.Background()` with a 2-minute timeout (the removed `timeoutTag` and goroutine). Now it calls `TagDevice` inline with the request context (line 44). Every anonymous request that misses the local cache waits for the upsert, plus the COUNT when `device_limit > 0`, before authentication returns. Nothing in this path sets a deadline on that context, so if the database stalls, anonymous requests stall with it until the client disconnects. Previously the write was bounded at 2 minutes and never delayed the response. The tagging call should keep a bounded context.
